newsitem.title: UK: Labour faces by-election as UK parliament recesses.
newsitem.headline: Labour faces by-election as UK parliament recesses.

text.p: British Prime Minister Tony Blair on Thursday faced the first major test of his popularity since winning power in elections on May 1 as the first session of a Labour-controlled parliament in 18 years came to an end.

Labour is narrowly favoured to win a parliamentary by-election in the traditionally Conservative seat of Uxbridge, which would increase its majority in the 659-seat House of Commons to a massive 180 seats.

History is against Labour winning Uxbridge as a governing party has not taken a seat from the main opposition party at a by-election since 1960. Also local Labour voters are angry that a candidate with no links to the area has been "imposed" on them.

But an opinion poll in the Times newspaper showed that Blair, welcomed nationally as a breath of fresh air and reforming energy after years of increasingly static Conservative rule, continued to enjoy a honeymoon with voters.

The MORI poll gave Labour 57 percent support, just one point down on its post-election peak, with the Conservatives at 23 percent, also a point down. At the May 1 election, Labour won 43.2 percent of the national vote.
The Uxbridge by-election was caused by the death of Conservative deputy Sir Michael Shersby, just seven days after he won the seat by only 724 votes. The result is due in the early hours of Friday.

With parliament closing for the summer recess on Thursday, Blair was set to cap three months of radical policy-making by announcing a tightening of the code of conduct for ministers to stem opposition charges that one of his team had a conflict of interest over a share portfolio.

At issue is the decision by David Simon to keep shares in oil giant British Petroleum after quitting as BP chairman upon joining the government as unpaid minister for trade and competiveness in Europe.

The new Conservative leader William Hague, who replaced former prime minister John Major after the party's election rout, fiercely attacked Blair on Wednesday in parliament for failing to avoid a conflict of interest and for "hypocrisy".

Minister without portfolio Peter Mandelson -- one of Blair's closest confidants -- told a BBC interviewer on Thursday that Simon could not sell his shares because of stringent insider trading rules and said the new minister had been careful to avoid any conflict of interest.
But he said the new code, to be published later on Thursday, would "make life harder for ministers and that's quite right, too."

"There will be new limits on gifts and hospitality received by ministers... We are not going to allow our ministers to fall to the standards of behaviour of some of those in the previous Tory (Conservative) administration."
A number of top Conservatives were accused of financial and sexual misconduct in the dying days of their administration, boosting Labour's victory prospects.
